title_en: How we detect frontier model misalignment
excerpt_en: OpenAI uses layered monitoring to detect frontier model misalignment and unauthorized agent behavior so responders can intervene before incidents escalate.
content_en:
# How we detect frontier model misalignment

As we train increasingly capable AI models, we need reliable ways to detect when their behavior departs from what we intended. Agents can misbehave and take unauthorized actions during training, evaluation, or deployment, with potentially serious consequences. In order to detect these failures—and, where necessary, to intervene in time—we monitor how agents reason, what actions they take, and how those actions affect their environment.

While we’ve been <u>monitoring our internal coding agents</u> for some time, the <u>Hugging Face incident</u> exposed a gap in our coverage: the incident began during internal cybersecurity evaluations on which we were not running our monitors for misaligned behavior. In response to that incident, and to the <u>increasing capabilities</u> of our models more generally, we’ve substantially expanded our system for monitoring agents’ behavior. Our misalignment monitors now cover our frontier models across a much wider variety of surfaces, including training, evaluation, internal use, and, with modifications depending on the product surface, external deployment.

In order to see how this expanded system could have helped prevent the Hugging Face incident, we replayed the behavior recorded in that episode with our strengthened monitors in place. In that simulation, our monitoring system alerted our security team about 30 minutes after the agents first escaped their sandbox—and more than 30 hours before Hugging Face’s systems were breached in the actual incident. We believe that this warning would have given our responders time to interrupt the activity well before our models were able to access external services.

In September, we saw how responders used an alert during a live training run. A model found a way to <u>reach the internet</u>(opens in a new window) from an environment that was meant to be isolated. Our monitors flagged the breach within 15 minutes, and a responder began reviewing it three minutes later. We then paused frontier reinforcement learning while we strengthened the systems that contain our agents.

While this monitoring system demands substantial compute, we think that cost is worth paying as our models become more capable and the potential consequences of model misalignment increase. Monitoring is one of several layers in our strategy of <u>defense in depth</u> against harm from misaligned model behavior. Alignment training aims to reduce models’ propensities toward harmful behavior; security controls <u>limit the systems an agent can access or affect</u>; and, when those safeguards fail, monitoring helps us detect the failures that remain, intervene before harm occurs, and learn from what went wrong. We believe that <u>all model developers</u> should monitor the behavior of their most capable models.

Below, we describe how our internal monitoring system works, what it has found so far, and how we’re evaluating and improving its performance.

For models at least as capable as GPT‑6 Astra, we monitor every reinforcement learning (RL) run and evaluation, as well as any harness that supports tool use. For most workloads, including RL and evaluations, we also monitor models we assess to be more capable than GPT‑5.5 Thinking. We also monitor all internal Codex traffic, regardless of the model being used. A version of this system also monitors external tool use for models above the Critical threshold for cybersecurity capabilities under our <u>Preparedness Framework</u>, as described below in this post.

In order to detect incidents while using compute efficiently, we’ve designed our monitoring system to follow a multilayer architecture. We spend relatively little compute on the first screening stages, where we want to catch as many concerning cases as we can: those stages are designed to pass cases along, even when the evidence is ambiguous. Later stages can spend more compute on each case to work out what happened, whether the model’s behavior is concerning, and whether we need to intervene.

Our initial layer (L0) uses lightweight classifiers we call *activation probes*. They look for concerning patterns in the model’s internal activations, and pass flagged cases to the next layer for review. We tune these probes for high recall, accepting some false alarms to reduce the chance of missing concerning behavior.

Because we’re still evaluating how well the probes detect unfamiliar forms of misalignment, we also send the next layer a random 5 percent of the traffic that our probes don’t flag. Reviewing that sample helps us identify concerning behavior the probes may have missed. Because of their sensitivity, we have our frontier RL runs and internal Codex traffic skip this layer and proceed directly to the next one.

At the next layer (L1), a model-based reviewer examines the agent’s recent conversation, chain of thought, and tool use. It looks for signs of deception, unauthorized actions, and attempts to manipulate an evaluation. The reviewer does this using the same context window the agent had when it acted. If the agent’s earlier work has been summarized for the context window under review, the reviewer sees that summary.

For frontier RL runs and internal Codex traffic, we run an L1 check at the end of each turn and whenever the agent summarizes its earlier work to make room in its context window. We are now moving to a schedule with no more than 30 minutes between these checks.

An agent’s actions can look quite different once we know what it was asked to do. When the L1 reviewer flags a case, it’s sent to our next layer (L2) for further inspection by our investigative agent. This investigative agent can check the purpose of an evaluation and, where the full transcript is available, read back across all of the agent’s context windows to see how it arrived at its actions. The investigative agent can also write and run code in an isolated environment to examine the relevant evidence. It then uses what it finds to reconstruct the incident, identify duplicate reports, and make a decision about how serious the case is.

We use different investigative agents for different purposes. Our security investigator looks for signs that someone may need to intervene—such as when an agent escaped its sandbox or accessed a system without authorization. Our alignment investigator, meanwhile, looks for behavior worth studying even when it poses no immediate security risk. Where both investigators are in use, each reviews every case flagged by our L1 layer. We are currently expanding the use of alignment investigations across our internal workloads.

For sensitive workloads, including internal Codex use, evaluations, and RL runs, a further check at our next layer (L3) draws on evidence outside the conversation. The security investigator compares the transcript with network logs, other system telemetry, and evidence from earlier cases to decide whether to alert a human responder. At L3, alignment reviewers also compare reports across cases to identify serious failures and recurring patterns, and examine frontier RL runs in greater depth.

For workloads that skip this layer, the L2 security investigator can alert responders directly.

When paging is enabled, the highest-priority security alerts reach members of our security and training teams, typically within 15 minutes of the initial alert. Responders review the evidence, examine the affected systems, and take action to contain the incident. How we follow up on less urgent findings, such as alignment failures that don’t pose immediate security risks, depends on the relevant workload.

False alarms have made it difficult to keep paging enabled around the clock for every workload. For frontier RL runs, a highest-priority alert can page a human responder at any hour. title_en: Ex-Palantir execs launch Dream with $17M from a16z to build AI world models for construction
excerpt_en: Dream is grounded in real physics and construction standards. Just as LLMs learn from text, Dream's world model is trained on more than 100 million square feet of building data gathered from permit archives across the United States.
content_en:
Andy Elder and Arjun Mathur were Stanford roommates who both studied computer science before spending a decade at Palantir. Elder led product design for a team of 800 people building software for U.S. defense and intelligence agencies, while Mathur served as a senior vice president in the company’s commercial practice. When the friends decided to build a startup early last year, there was no question they would do it together.

Despite having no direct background in architecture, Elder and Mathur were troubled by a growing problem: Fewer buildings are constructed in the U.S. today than a few decades ago, as development costs have surged.

“We’ve gone from dial-up internet to superintelligent AI, but our ability to build the physical world around us has actually decreased,” Mathur told TechCrunch.

Believing AI can boost productivity across the architecture, engineering, and construction (AEC) industry, they set out to build Dream, a startup developing built world models that automate building design and engineering. Dream has emerged from stealth with $17 million in seed funding led by Andreessen Horowitz, alongside other backers, including SV Angel, XYZ, and Zigg Capital. The startup aims to replace cumbersome, outdated AEC tools like Autodesk’s AutoCAD and Revit.

If you sit next to an architect or a structural engineer, you’ll notice that they are still “drawing” every piece of their designs part by part on legacy software, Mathur said. “AI really plays no role in that equation.”

While a standard LLM like ChatGPT can generate an image of a building, the result won’t be structurally sound. Dream, by contrast, is grounded in real physics and construction standards. Just as LLMs learn from text, Dream’s world model is trained on more than 100 million square feet of building data gathered from permit archives across the United States.

“Our model actually understands what’s within those walls. What materials are used, what the beams are made of, and how much weight they can support,” Elder said.

The startup calls its approach “structural cognition” because its model generates structurally precise designs that account for internal building elements like plumbing and HVAC.

Dream has already begun selling its product to AEC professionals and developers, who use the model to conceptualize building designs and estimate overall costs, according to the founders. The platform is already deployed across 10 active projects in Texas and California.

While Dream isn’t the only company attempting to update AEC software with AI — other startups working on this include Motif, Snaptrude, and Arcol — Elder and Mathur claim that they are the only ones that developed a world model that instantly designs whole buildings.

Kimberly Tan, a partner at Andreessen Horowitz, said that while the firm first invested in Dream over a year ago, when the startup model was just an idea, she has been extremely impressed with their progress. “I have not seen anybody take the technical approach,” she said. “They’re doing everything based on their own models.”

content_en:
Meta has quietly launched Style Sketch, an AI fashion app that helps users put together outfit ideas using clothes they already own. The app connects to Instagram to build a virtual closet from photos you’ve posted, or lets you add items manually by snapping a photo, recording a quick video, or uploading images from your camera roll.

Style Sketch then suggests outfit combinations built from your wardrobe matched to your style. Users can then try on the outfits on a “realistic model matched to your body shape and skin tone,” the app description reads.

The app, which was first spotted by social media consultant Matt Navarra, is available in Indonesia, Singapore, and Thailand on iOS and Android.

Meta did not respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment. It’s unknown whether Meta plans to launch Style Sketch more widely.

Several apps already use AI to help users digitize their wardrobes and visualize new outfits, including startups like Alta. Even Google Photos offers tools that let users turn photos of their clothes into digital closets where they can create new outfit ideas.

To compete with what’s already on the market, Meta will likely rely less on the novelty of the idea and more on the app’s integration with Instagram, where users already have a visual record of their personal style.

Rather than relying on random suggestions, users can also select a specific item from their wardrobe and get fresh outfit ideas built around it, according to the app description.

The app can also help users plan outfits for trips. If they enter their destination, trip length and planned activities, users can get a day-by-day outfit plan that takes the weather forecast and itinerary into account.

Style Sketch is one of many AI apps from Meta in recent months. Most recently, the company launched an app called Waddle World, which essentially looks like a Tamagotchi clone, but with AI. Meta has also launched Pocket, a tool for vibe-coding games, and Vibes, which lets users quickly generate AI-powered videos.

The wave of new apps is part of a broader effort at Meta to release more apps. The Wall Street Journal reported earlier this year that CEO Mark Zuckerberg told employees the company plans to release far more apps than it has historically, as AI-driven efficiencies have made it faster and easier to ship new apps.

content_en:
A top executive of a Singapore AI cloud firm that was accused of illegally selling Nvidia chips to China could also have been a Chinese spy, anonymous sources told the New York Times.

The executive, Alice Huang (or Huang Le), worked for Megaspeed and was photographed as one of multiple people hanging out with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang during various business dinners in the Singapore region. U.S. intelligence agencies had been surveilling Alice Huang to learn more about her ties with China for about a year, the Times reports.

The concern, sources said, was that Alice Huang had grown so close to Jensen Huang that she could have been gathering information about Nvidia’s plans and the CEO’s efforts to convince the Trump administration to allow it to ship more advanced technology to China.

But an Nvidia spokesperson denied this, telling TechCrunch that the CEO’s relationship with the Megaspeed executive was the same as with any other regional customer.

“Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a C.E.O.’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” the spokesperson said in an emailed statement. The company also said, “Our regional cloud customers receive ordinary business information — not sensitive NVIDIA trade secrets — and zero information relevant to national security.”

In 2025, the Times reported that the Commerce Department had investigated Megaspeed over concerns that it was helping Chinese companies sidestep AI chip export regulations by reselling restricted chips to them. Alice Huang was said to be a top executive for the firm at the time.

content_en:
**Bleu Robotics**, a Paris-based startup building AI models for industrial humanoid robots, has raised a €5 million pre-Seed round, to reach its goal of reducing the full humanoid robot deployment process to one hour or shorter.

The round was co-led by Contrarian Ventures and OVNI Capital, with participation from Kvanted, WEPA Ventures, Motier Ventures and Charlie Songhurst, and board members at Meta.

**Benoît Berkoukchi**, co-founder of Bleu Robotics, says, “*Humanoid robots in manufacturing are the next automotive sector, with the potential to help Europe and the US reshore production. But most robotics companies are trying to train humanoids with millions of data points and build fully general-purpose models. That approach isn’t suited to manufacturing. There isn’t enough data on factory work, and there won’t be internet-scale data, the kind LLMs were built on, for robots for a long time. Our methodology means we can do more with less*.”

The round comes amid continued European investment in robotics software, humanoid systems and Physical AI during 2026.

In France, Paris-based Inbolt raised €11 million to expand its hardware-agnostic robot intelligence platform, while Norway- and US-based Trener Robotics secured €26 million to develop AI-powered skills for industrial robots.

Elsewhere, Belgium’s Motion raised €1.7 million for humanoid deployment, Spain’s THEKER secured €73 million to scale generalist industrial robotics, and London-based Humanoid raised €133 million for its industrial humanoid platform.

Together with funding rounds for Germany’s Sereact, Switzerland’s Enact Intelligence and Poland’s Nomagic, these financings total €372.7 million in 2026, rising to €377.7 million when including Bleu Robotics’ latest round.

**Thomas Poitrineau**, Investor at Contrarian Ventures, adds, “*We were attracted to Bleu Robotics because of their ambitious choice to rethink how humanoid robotics software should work from first principles. It’s rare to find a company led by two world-class robotics researchers and a manufacturing expert, which is also why their software works differently from their competition. Their goal is far bigger than simply making the best model in a lab. It’s an approach that can already scale, putting robots to work in factories within months rather than years*.”

Founded in Paris in 2025 by two INRIA researchers and a former Renault manufacturing manager, Bleu’s abductive learning technology reportedly lets robots learn new tasks from only a handful of operator demonstrations.

Its software runs on any humanoid platform and includes the AI model and training devices needed to teach robots on the factory floor.

According to the International Federation of Robotics, there were 5 million industrial robots operating globally in 2025. However, these robots are built to repeat fixed tasks, and are unable to adapt to the high-mix, low-volume production now common in modern manufacturing, so that work still falls to human workers.

Humanoid robots are needed to automate a wider range of complex tasks. While hardware has advanced significantly in recent years, software development has struggled to keep pace, limiting real-world deployment.

Interact Analysis found that of the 20,000-plus humanoids produced last year, only 10% reached real-world applications. Most of these robots today rely on end-to-end models, which learn everything in a single black box and require massive amounts of data to achieve production-ready reliability.

As a result, deployment remains costly and time-consuming for manufacturers, often requiring hundreds of hours of training data, with no guarantee the robot will perform reliably.

Instead of an end-to-end model, Bleu Robotics’ abductive learning model allows the robot to learn a new task from as few as ten operator demonstrations, while keeping the explainability required for industrial safety and the 99%+ accuracy that production lines demand.

### Motion Picture Association runs its legal operations on a CRM built for sales

Legal operations teams are finding that software built for sales pipelines can just as easily run investigations and member communications. As AI agents take on triage work, even nontechnical teams are building those workflows themselves.

That shift is playing out at the Motion Picture Association Inc., where a CRM module on monday.com Ltd.’s AI work platform now anchors piracy investigations and content protection cases. It links offices in Asia-Pacific, Europe, Latin America, Canada and the U.S., according to Melisa King (pictured), legal operations administrator and senior paralegal at the MPA.

“We have a lot of players in the kitchen, and the CRM module helps us communicate not just internally but externally,” King said. “So our members can have real-time information, find out what’s missing, if there’s documents they need to sign, and it really just helps us move the beast.”

King spoke with Rebecca Knight at monday.com’s Elevate event, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how the MPA tracks anti-piracy cases, how an AI agent triages security alerts and why CRM isn’t just for sales. *(\* Disclosure below.)*

### AI triage lightens the legal operations load

Every case starts with a person. A tip comes in, an investigator checks it and the case goes onto a board, where the team weighs a takedown, a cease-and-desist letter or litigation. Studio powers of attorney are tracked there too, so investigators know where they can act, King explained.

“I think before, each region really worked independently from one another, and this has allowed us to collaborate and work together,” she said.

The newest addition is an AI agent, the kind of tool monday.com is having every Elevate attendee build. It triages security advisories for the Trusted Partner Network, which vets editing bays, before a point person decides who needs a follow-up. King tested it before launch and built it without a coding background.

“I think with anyone, we get hundreds of emails a day and it’s really easy to ignore these alerts,” she said.

For a small legal operations team, the payoff is time, efficiency and analytics showing members how many cases were stopped before litigation. King’s advice to teams that see CRM as a sales-only tool is to think bigger.

“I would say to think of it as project management on steroids with the communication aspect tied to it,” King said. “The communication is key because it keeps everyone connected, especially when people are working remote or hybrid or around the world.”

Until earlier in the year, the play was around having a focused app that does one thing well. But now, all of these apps are thinking about how to get more out of capturing users’ speech.

content_en:
Swedish AI startup **Pixel Systems** has raised €2.7 million ($3.1 million) in a Seed round to accelerate their commercial initiatives and continue building the technology that helps identify AI-generated and manipulated images, documents, and other digital material.

The round was led by Unconventional Ventures, at a pre-money valuation of approximately €18 million ($21 million).

“*Generative AI has made it extremely cheap to fabricate evidence. The problem is that almost every digital process still rests on the assumption that what people submit is authentic. That assumption is disappearing,*” says **Robel Efrem**, co-founder and CEO of Pixel.

Pixel’s funding follows other European investments in digital trust and fraud-prevention technology reported by EU-Startups in 2026, including Sweden’s Bits (€12 million), Denmark’s Flare (€3.6 million), France’s Marble (€6.5 million) and MokN (€12.9 million), Spain’s Zepo Intelligence (€12.8 million), and UK/Germany-based Diligent AI (€2.1 million).

Together, these rounds represent approximately €49.9 million in funding, excluding Pixel’s €2.7 million Seed round, across companies addressing different aspects of verification, fraud prevention and financial crime.

EU-Startups previously covered Efrem as co-founder and CEO of Swedish esports platform Challengermode, which raised €10.1 million in 2020.

“*We believe the ability to verify digital information will become as natural a part of tomorrow’s infrastructure as cybersecurity is today. That a Swedish company has the opportunity to take a leading position in this field is exactly the kind of development we want to help make possible,*” adds **Nora Bavey**, General Partner at Unconventional Ventures.

Founded in 2026 in Stockholm, Pixel develops proprietary technology to detect AI-generated and manipulated digital content. By combining several independent forensic analysis methods, Pixel helps companies verify images, documents, and other digital material before it is used as the basis for decisions, payouts, or other critical processes.

The team behind Pixel consists of senior engineers, AI specialists, and competitive programmers.

In Pixel’s internal tests, the platform has achieved a detection rate of 99.98 percent for AI-generated and manipulated material, reportedly placing the technology at a world-leading level.

Pixel is used today in businesses where digital material forms the basis for financial decisions, including insurance, FinTech, e-commerce, and professional services.

Use cases include manipulated damage photos in insurance claims, fabricated receipts and invoices, AI-generated product images in refund fraud, and manipulated material in financial or legal processes.

“*The internet was built for a world where an image could largely be treated as proof. That world no longer exists. Now every company that receives images, receipts, and documents from its customers needs to be able to check that material before money is paid out,*” says **Robel Efrem**.

The funding comes just months after the company was founded. Three weeks after its commercial launch, Pixel has reached its first €89k ($100k) in contracted recurring revenue.

content_en:
*The New York Times* is testing a new AI feature for its Cooking app that helps users to modify recipes, and it has sparked some drama among users. Last Friday, *NYT* Cooking senior editor Genevieve Ko announced the feature, which can be used to recommend substitutions for ingredients and cooking equipment, scale recipes to any number of servings, and “generally make our recipes work for what a cook needs at that moment.”

# The NYT Cooking app is testing AI recipe modifications

Some users aren’t exactly thrilled with The New York Times’ recipe-tweaking AI tool.

One of the examples given in the article shows a user asking to use baby spinach instead of kale, with the Cooking app feature advising that because baby spinach wilts faster, it should be added during a later step of the recipe. Ko says it can also change the recipes around different pans and tools. Customized recipes are private and can’t be published or shared through the app. The AI modification feature is being rolled out gradually while the *NYT* monitors how it performs — it’s currently available to all Cooking subscribers on the iOS app, and it will be more broadly available “soon.”

Some *NYT* readers have pushed back against the feature, citing concerns in the article’s comment section around the environmental impact of widespread AI adoption and the general impact that AI features may have on the user experience. When one user asked if there will be a way to disable the AI feature, Ko responded with, “No, not at this time,” and noted that the feature is “completely optional to use.”

“Unbelievably disappointing to see,” said another *NYT* user. “I’ve always loved NYT Cooking and it pains me that the AI mandate has reached what used to be a wonderful and simple collection of recipes and notes from all sorts of different people.”

This isn’t the first time that AI has been used by the NYT Cooking app. Ko says it was used to convert imperial volume measurements to metric weight measurements in recipes two years ago, and a feature was added last year that converts recipes to halve or double the original serving size. The comments on the new AI feature announcement post have since been closed, but *NYT* spokesperson Jordan Cohen tells *The Verge* that this is standard practice:

“Comments on this article remained open for four days, with editors from Cooking taking care to answer questions, address concerns and engage directly with readers. We kept that conversation open to give readers a meaningful opportunity to share feedback and hear from the team. Closing comments on older articles is standard practice at The Times so that our moderators can focus on new discussions. We’re pleased to see that many members of our Cooking community are interested in exploring this tool and are already trying it out on our iOS app; they’re reporting good results.”
